summary:
Ouranos is a health monitoring system for astronauts that we built and tested in one weekend. It has three working parts: a watchOS app that reads more than 30 health measurements, a 3D-printed shroud and chain band that fit the Apple Watch SE and work with gloves, and a live mission dashboard.

The watch streams heart rate, breathing, heart-rate variability, motion and sleep data to the dashboard every 5 seconds after a one-time pairing code. When readings need review, the watch taps the wrist. The dashboard then shows what changed, which readings set off the flag, and the NASA guidance that applies, drawn from NASA-STD-3001 and the Human Research Program. Every answer links its NASA source.

This matters most far from Earth. Near Mars a message home can take 22 minutes each way, so the crew has to catch changes like the heart-rate rise behind orthostatic intolerance on their own. Ouranos gives the crew medical officer the evidence to do that. It never diagnoses. It flags what changed, shows why, and leaves the decision to the crew.
details:
Links
Presentation: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1B3vAlBLJ-Cv1vjAJwRmfYlrkPYke0u7M/view?usp=sharing

Live dashboard: https://useouranos.vercel.app

Source code: https://github.com/unfound-2/Ouranos_Nasa-Space-Apps

Demo video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ake4CKNaCjI

What it does

Ouranos monitors a crew member's health from the wrist and tells the crew medical officer when something changes, with the evidence and the matching NASA guidance attached. We built three parts that work together: a watchOS app, a 3D-printed wrist unit for the Apple Watch SE, and a mission dashboard on the web. A versioned data contract and a hosted API connect them.

The watch app

The app reads more than 30 measurements from Apple Health, plus wrist motion from Core Motion. These include heart rate, resting and walking heart rate, heart-rate recovery, heart-rate variability, respiration, VO2 max, sleep, steps, walking and running metrics, noise exposure and time in daylight. It syncs to the dashboard every 5 seconds.

The Home screen is a map of the body. Tap the chest for heart and breathing, or tap the legs for steps and walking.

A Sim mode plays a feed modelled on the Canadian Space Agency's Bio-Monitor, the smart shirt astronauts wear on the ISS, so the whole system can be shown without a crew. Every screen that shows simulated data says so.

Pairing and security

The watch asks the API for a pairing code, and the crew member enters their name and the 10-character code on the dashboard. A code works once and expires after 5 minutes, and pairing attempts are rate limited. Each watch gets its own token and the browser gets a 12-hour session. The database stores only hashes of codes and tokens, never the raw values. Only a paired browser can read that watch's readings.

How a flag is raised

Readings travel as small JSON frames. Each frame has a version, source, timestamp, simulated flag and list of readings. Each reading has a metric, value, unit, quality (valid or missing) and status (nominal, review or priority).

The watch drops stale frames and missing readings. It raises a review signal when any reading is priority, or when two or more readings stay in review for two frames in a row. The two-frame rule stops a single spike from a loose strap or a sudden movement from setting off an alert. A signal is not repeated while the same readings stay flagged, so one event means one buzz.

When a signal fires, the watch taps the wrist and sends the flagged readings to the dashboard as evidence. In this build the rules run on the Sim feed. Running them on live readings, measured against each crew member's own baseline, is the next step.

The dashboard

- Mission health: live heart-rate and breathing charts, a "What needs attention" panel and the readings behind the current flag. The 3D astronaut's suit details turn gold while something is flagged.

- Health review: what changed since the previous readings, and an assistant that answers questions such as "What changed?" in plain words and links the NASA guide that applies. It runs on Groq (openai/gpt-oss-20b) and falls back to the bundled guide text if the model can't be reached.

- Crew guide: health topics built on NASA standards and research, each linked to its NASA source.

- Daily plan: the day's activities and protected sleep time. From the watch, the crew member answers "How are you feeling?" and marks tasks done or running late. The check-in then appears on the dashboard for review.

- Monitoring systems: the paired watch and the other monitoring systems.

The wrist unit

The band is a parametric CAD model written in Python with build123d, so any dimension can be changed and the part reprinted. It has:

- an octagonal shroud with OURANOS engraved on the bezel;

- a slide-in back plate in five fit sizes (-0.6 mm to +0.6 mm), with a window that keeps the heart sensor on the skin;

- a print-in-place chain band;

- a pull tab big enough to grab with gloves on.

The crown, side button, microphone and speaker stay uncovered. Everything prints in PLA on an Elegoo Neptune 4 Pro without supports (0.2 mm layers, 4 walls, 40% gyroid infill). The bands attach with pins cut from 1.75 mm filament. The first fit test was printed on 14 November.

What makes it different

- The body is the interface. Readings are grouped by body region, so a glance at the wrist tells the crew where to look.

- Every flag shows its work. The dashboard lists the readings that caused it and links the NASA source, so the crew medical officer can check the reasoning instead of trusting a score.

- We built the software and hardware together. A commercial watch in a printed shroud becomes a light crew monitor that works with gloves.

- The data is honest. Simulated readings are always labelled. Channels the SE can't measure (blood oxygen, blood pressure and live skin temperature) appear only in the simulated feed.

What we considered

- Distance. Near Mars a message to Earth takes up to about 22 minutes each way, so a flight surgeon can't watch in real time. The review rules run on the watch itself, and the crew sees the flag first.

- Alert fatigue. A monitor that buzzes too often gets taken off. The two-frame rule and the no-repeat rule exist for that reason.

- Privacy. Health data is personal, even in orbit. We used single-use codes, per-watch tokens, rate limits and hashed storage.

- Gloves. The pull tab is sized for gloved hands, and the crown and side button stay uncovered.

- Who decides. Ouranos never diagnoses or clears anyone. It points the crew medical officer to the evidence and the NASA guidance, and the call stays with them.

Impact

Long missions will need crews to look after their own health. Ouranos shows that a light commercial watch, a printed shroud and clear software can catch slow changes and put them in front of the crew medical officer, with NASA's guidance next to them. Examples are a rising resting heart rate, poor sleep, or the heart-rate jump on standing that signals orthostatic intolerance after landing. A flight surgeon on Earth can review the same record later. The same setup could serve people who work far from a doctor on Earth, such as crews at polar research stations or on analog missions.

Built with

- Watch app: Swift, SwiftUI, HealthKit and Core Motion.

- Dashboard: TypeScript, React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Recharts and three.js.

- API: Express and Zod on a Vercel serverless function, with Supabase for storage and Groq for the assistant.

- Band: Python and build123d, printed on an Elegoo Neptune 4 Pro.

- Tests: around 300 unit tests in Vitest and 30 end-to-end tests in Playwright.

- Video: Remotion.

We used SI coding assistants, Claude (Anthropic) and OpenAI Codex, under our direction. Every SI-assisted part is listed in docs/AI_DISCLOSURE.md in the repo, and the demo video carries an SI-ASSISTED watermark.

Next steps

- Run the review rules on live readings, measured against each crew member's own baseline.

- Add blood oxygen and blood pressure from watches and patches that measure them. The data contract already carries those channels.

- Wear-test the band over full days and on an analog mission.

Team

- Dhruv: web dashboard, API and data contract.

- Mustafa: watch app and hosted pairing.

- Sriyan: the 3D-printed band and the demo video.
